newsitem.title: USA: INMETCO to expand cadmium battery recycling.
newsitem.headline: INMETCO to expand cadmium battery recycling.

text.p: INMETCO, the Inco Ltd subsidiary, is to spend $3.7 million on increasing its ability to recycle nickel-cadmium batteries at its site in Ellwood City, Pennsylvania, the company's national account manager, John Liotta said.
INMETCO began recycling spent nickel-cadmium batteries, the first to do so in the U.S., in December 1995, and invested $5 million to intall four furnaces. The facility has space for 16 furnaces.

The company processed 3,000 tonnes of spent batteries last year, but with the expansion this will rise to 3,500 to 3,600 tonnes this year, still only 10 to 15 percent of nickel cadmium batteries made in the U.S. Some spent batteries are imported from Europe, Liotta told delegates at Metal Bulletin's Minor Metals Seminar here.
Battery recycling organisations estimate that by 2002, half of all nickel cadmium batteries made in the U.S. will be recycled.
The average cadmium metal content of each battery is 12 to 15 percent. Recycled cadmium is a minimum 99.95 percent pure used to make new batteries.
Some 80 to 85 percent of cadmium is used in batteries for power tools and other appliances.
"The growth of usage for cadmium batteries in the U.S. is rather flat at this time. Of course the big question is what battery chemistry will go into electric vehicles," Liotta said.
Several metals are jostling for orders in the electric vehicle battery race.
The nickel recovered from the spent batteries is sold to stainless steel producers.
Inco is also looking at recycling lithium ion batteries to extract the cobalt oxide used in the first wave.
